claim: Listeners with normal hearing show considerable individual differences in speech understanding when competing speakers are present.
source: Listeners with normal hearing show considerable individual differences in speech understanding when competing speakers are present, as in a crowded restaurant.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about the phenomenon being studied.

claim: Individual differences in the ability to focus selective attention on a target stimulus in the presence of distractors are associated with sentence identification in the presence of spatially separated competing speakers.
source: In 50 young normal-hearing listeners, the performance in tasks measuring auditory and visual selective attention was associated with sentence identification in the presence of spatially separated competing speakers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data with 50 participants.

claim: Measures of selective attention explained a similar proportion of variance as the binaural sensitivity for the acoustic temporal fine structure.
source: Together, the measures of selective attention explained a similar proportion of variance as the binaural sensitivity for the acoustic temporal fine structure.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of variance explained by different predictors in the study.

claim: Working memory span showed no significant association with speech understanding in the cocktail-party task.
source: Working memory span, age, and audiometric thresholds showed no significant association with speech understanding.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by regression analysis results.

claim: Age showed no significant association with speech understanding in the cocktail-party task.
source: Working memory span, age, and audiometric thresholds showed no significant association with speech understanding.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by regression analysis results.

claim: Audiometric thresholds showed no significant association with speech understanding in the cocktail-party task.
source: Working memory span, age, and audiometric thresholds showed no significant association with speech understanding.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by regression analysis results.

claim: A reduced ability to focus attention on a target is one reason why some listeners with normal hearing sensitivity have difficulty communicating in situations with background noise.
source: These results suggest that a reduced ability to focus attention on a target is one reason why some listeners with normal hearing sensitivity have difficulty communicating in situations with background noise.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings presented in the abstract.

claim: The human auditory system has impressive abilities in structuring the mixture of sound waves arriving at the ears into different auditory objects or streams.
source: While the human auditory system has impressive abilities in structuring the mixture of sound waves arriving at the ears into different auditory objects or streams (auditory scene analysis; e.g., Bregman, 1990; Carlyon, 2004), listeners show considerable variation when it comes to speech understanding in adverse acoustic conditions, such as the almost proverbial 'cocktail-party' situation described above (Bronkhorst, 2000; Cherry, 1953).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established work in auditory scene analysis.

claim: Listeners show considerable variation in speech understanding in adverse acoustic conditions such as cocktail-party situations.
source: While the human auditory system has impressive abilities in structuring the mixture of sound waves arriving at the ears into different auditory objects or streams (auditory scene analysis; e.g., Bregman, 1990; Carlyon, 2004), listeners show considerable variation when it comes to speech understanding in adverse acoustic conditions, such as the almost proverbial 'cocktail-party' situation described above (Bronkhorst, 2000; Cherry, 1953).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on cocktail-party listening.

claim: Pronounced individual differences in speech identification in background noise are observed even in listeners with normal hearing.
source: Surprisingly, pronounced individual differences in speech identification in background noise are observed even in listeners with normal hearing, that is, with audiometric thresholds better than 20 dB HL within the frequency range most important for speech (100 Hz–4 kHz; Byrne et al., 1994), usually taken as an indication of approximately intact processing in the inner ear.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation to support the frequency range definition.

claim: The frequency range 100 Hz–4 kHz is most important for speech.
source: Surprisingly, pronounced individual differences in speech identification in background noise are observed even in listeners with normal hearing, that is, with audiometric thresholds better than 20 dB HL within the frequency range most important for speech (100 Hz–4 kHz; Byrne et al., 1994), usually taken as an indication of approximately intact processing in the inner ear.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Byrne et al., 1994.

claim: In a simulated cocktail-party listening task with two competing speakers presented 15° to the left and right of the target speaker, the percentage of correct responses in reporting a sequence of digits varied between 40% and 85% across normal-hearing listeners in an anechoic condition.
source: For example, Ruggles and Shinn-Cunningham (2011) tested normal-hearing subjects in a simulated cocktail-party listening task with two competing speakers presented 15° to the left and right of the target speaker. Across listeners, the percentage of correct responses in reporting a sequence of digits produced by the target speaker varied between 40% and 85% in an anechoic condition.
evidence: This is data from a cited study by Ruggles and Shinn-Cunningham (2011).

claim: A relevant number of patients with normal audiometric findings complain about hearing difficulties in daily life.
source: Compatible with these experimental results, in clinical settings a relevant number of patients with normal audiometric findings complain about hearing difficulties in daily life (Zhao and Stephens, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhao and Stephens, 2007.

claim: Understanding speech in a cocktail-party situation with interfering speakers and other background noise requires selective attention.
source: Understanding speech in a cocktail-party situation with interfering speakers and other background noise requires selective attention (Bronkhorst, 2015; Cherry, 1953; Shinn-Cunningham, 2008; Xiang et al., 2010), and was even proposed to be the 'best-known real life example of selective attention' (Pashler, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Cocktail-party listening was proposed to be the 'best-known real life example of selective attention'.
source: Understanding speech in a cocktail-party situation with interfering speakers and other background noise requires selective attention (Bronkhorst, 2015; Cherry, 1953; Shinn-Cunningham, 2008; Xiang et al., 2010), and was even proposed to be the 'best-known real life example of selective attention' (Pashler, 1998).
evidence: This is a claim attributed to Pashler, 1998.

claim: Several aspects of speech appear to be processed outside the focus of attention.
source: Although several aspects of speech appear to be processed outside the focus of attention (Pulvermüller and Shtyrov, 2006), attention enhances the representation of speech (and other sounds) at relatively early stages (e.g., Choi et al., 2014; Srinivasan et al., 2012; Xiang et al., 2010; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pulvermüller and Shtyrov, 2006.

claim: Attention enhances the representation of speech and other sounds at relatively early stages.
source: Although several aspects of speech appear to be processed outside the focus of attention (Pulvermüller and Shtyrov, 2006), attention enhances the representation of speech (and other sounds) at relatively early stages (e.g., Choi et al., 2014; Srinivasan et al., 2012; Xiang et al., 2010; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Speech identification performance is better when the listener knows in advance which of three talkers would be the target speaker, compared to conditions where the target location is uncertain.
source: For instance, in an experiment by Kidd et al. (2005); the speech identification performance was better when the listener knew in advance which of three talkers (presented at different spatial positions) would be the target speaker, compared to conditions where the target location was uncertain.
evidence: This is data from a cited study by Kidd et al. (2005).

claim: Being able to direct attention to the correct location results in a large improvement in speech recognition for exactly identical acoustic signals.
source: Thus, for exactly identical acoustic signals, being able to direct attention to the correct location results in a large improvement in speech recognition (e.g., Best et al., 2007; Kitterick et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Best et al., 2007 and Kitterick et al., 2010.

claim: The direction of selective attention to the target speaker can be impaired due to limitations imposed by the acoustic signal or by perceptual or cognitive characteristics of the listener.
source: The direction of selective attention to the target speaker can be impaired due to limitations imposed by the acoustic signal or by perceptual or cognitive characteristics of the listener (cf. Mattys et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mattys et al., 2012.

claim: Most previous studies on attention and speech understanding in noise used tests developed for neuropsychological settings.
source: Surprisingly, this particular aspect of attention has not been studied very systematically in previous experiments that investigated the role of attention for speech understanding in noise (Füllgrabe et al., 2014; Gatehouse and Akeroyd, 2008; Heinrich et al., 2015; Neher et al., 2009, 2011, 2012; Schoof and Rosen, 2014; van Rooij et al., 1989). Most of these studies used tests developed for neuropsychological settings, like the Test of Everyday Attention (TEA; Robertson et al., 1996) and the Trail Making Tests (TMT; Bowie and Harvey, 2006), indexing visual search (TEA Map Search, Telephone Search), task/attentional switching (TEA Visual Elevator and Auditory Elevator with Reversal, TMT-B), sustained attention (TMT-A, TEA Lottery Test and Elevator Counting), or divided attention (TEA Telephone Search While Counting).
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research with multiple citations.

claim: Only one TEA subtest ('Elevator counting with distraction') directly addresses the capability to ignore distractors.
source: Only one TEA subtest ("Elevator counting with distraction") directly addresses the capability to ignore distractors.
evidence: This is an assessment of the TEA test battery based on the authors' analysis.

claim: Only two studies included the 'Elevator counting with distraction' subtest in hearing-impaired listeners.
source: We are aware of only two studies that included this subtest (Gatehouse and Akeroyd, 2008; Neher et al., 2009), in hearing-impaired listeners.
evidence: This is based on the authors' review of the literature with citations.

claim: If a target sound is followed by a backward masker after a silent inter-stimulus interval of 50 ms or more, it is virtually impossible that the masker affects the representation of the target in the auditory nerve.
source: If – as in the present study – a target sound is followed by a backward masker after a silent inter-stimulus interval (ISI) of 50 ms or more, it is virtually impossible that the masker affects the representation of the target in the auditory nerve (Kiang et al., 1965; Plack and Viemeister, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kiang et al., 1965 and Plack and Viemeister, 1992.

claim: Strong effects of the backward masker on intensity discrimination can be explained by a failure to selectively attend to the target sounds while ignoring the maskers.
source: Instead, strong effects of the backward masker on intensity discrimination can be explained by a failure to selectively attend to the target sounds while ignoring the maskers (Oberfeld and Stahn, 2012; Oberfeld et al., 2012; Schlauch et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research including the authors' own work.

claim: In a study using behavioral reverse-correlation, the effect of non-simultaneous masking on the intensity difference limen was well accounted for by the attention to the maskers, explaining 72% of the variance.
source: For example, in a study from our lab that quantified the amount of attention directed to the maskers using a behavioral reverse-correlation approach (Oberfeld et al., 2014), the effect of non-simultaneous masking on the intensity difference limen (DL) was well accounted for by the attention to the maskers, explaining 72% of the variance.
evidence: This is data from a cited study by the authors (Oberfeld et al., 2014).

claim: Listeners with normal audiometric thresholds may differ in their sensitivity to the temporal fine structure of sounds.
source: Listeners with normal audiometric thresholds may differ in their sensitivity to the temporal fine structure (TFS) of sounds (e.g., Füllgrabe, 2013; Ruggles et al., 2011), which is necessary for using interaural time difference (ITD) cues to sound localization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Füllgrabe, 2013 and Ruggles et al., 2011.

claim: Temporal fine structure sensitivity is necessary for using interaural time difference cues to sound localization.
source: Listeners with normal audiometric thresholds may differ in their sensitivity to the temporal fine structure (TFS) of sounds (e.g., Füllgrabe, 2013; Ruggles et al., 2011), which is necessary for using interaural time difference (ITD) cues to sound localization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the role of TFS.

claim: Differences in TFS sensitivity were proposed to be due to cochlear neuropathy, which could be caused by moderate noise exposure.
source: These differences were proposed to be due to cochlear neuropathy, which could for instance be caused by moderate noise exposure (Bharadwaj et al., 2015; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009) and is sometimes described as 'hidden hearing loss' (Plack et al., 2014) because it cannot be detected using standard measures of audiometric threshold.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Bharadwaj et al., 2015 and Kujawa and Liberman, 2009.

claim: Cochlear neuropathy is sometimes described as 'hidden hearing loss' because it cannot be detected using standard measures of audiometric threshold.
source: These differences were proposed to be due to cochlear neuropathy, which could for instance be caused by moderate noise exposure (Bharadwaj et al., 2015; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009) and is sometimes described as 'hidden hearing loss' (Plack et al., 2014) because it cannot be detected using standard measures of audiometric threshold.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Plack et al., 2014.

claim: Several studies showed a correlation between TFS sensitivity and the recognition of speech in noise, for normal-hearing as well as for hearing-impaired listeners.
source: Several studies showed a correlation between TFS sensitivity and the recognition of speech in noise, for normal-hearing as well as for hearing-impaired listeners (Bharadwaj et al., 2015; Füllgrabe et al., 2014; Neher et al., 2011, 2012; Ruggles et al., 2011; Schoof and Rosen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The regression model showed a good fit with R² = 0.57, p<0.001, N = 45.
source: The regression model showed a good fit, R2 = 0.57, p<0.001, N = 45.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's regression analysis.

claim: Performance in the cocktail-party listening task was significantly negatively related to the intensity-DL elevation under backward masking.
source: As can be seen in Table 1, the performance in the cocktail-party listening task was significantly negatively related to the intensity-DL elevation under backward masking.
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Participants who showed a better capability of focusing attention on the target sounds in the intensity discrimination task were less affected by the interfering speakers in the cocktail-party listening task.
source: Thus, compatible with our hypotheses, participants who showed a better capability of focusing attention on the target sounds in the intensity discrimination task were less affected by the interfering speakers in the cocktail-party listening task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative regression coefficient for DLelev.

claim: The significant negative regression coefficient for flanker interference shows that a high capability of directing visual selective attention corresponded to good performance on the cocktail-party listening task.
source: In the same line of reasoning, the significant negative regression coefficient for flanker interference shows that a high capability of directing visual selective attention corresponded to good performance on the cocktail-party listening task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression coefficient for IntFlanker shown in Table 1.

claim: The IPD threshold measured in the TFS-LF task was significantly negatively related to the SRS.
source: The IPD threshold measured in the TFS-LF task was also significantly negatively related to the SRS.
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Listeners who showed high sensitivity for the TFS performed better in the spatial listening task.
source: Thus, compatible with previous studies (e.g., Füllgrabe et al., 2014; Neher et al., 2011, 2012; Ruggles et al., 2012), listeners who showed high sensitivity for the TFS performed better in the spatial listening task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression result with reference to previous studies.

claim: The general dominance weight was highest for the IPD threshold in the TFS-LF task, followed by the DL-elevation in the intensity discrimination task.
source: As shown in Table 1, the general dominance weight was highest for the IPD threshold in the TFS-LF task, followed by the DL-elevation in the intensity discrimination task.
evidence: This is a result from the dominance analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: According to dominance analysis, sensitivity for the binaural TFS and auditory selective attention are the most important predictors of cocktail-party listening.
source: According to these results, sensitivity for the binaural TFS and auditory selective attention are the most important predictors of cocktail-party listening.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dominance analysis results.

claim: The Lasso method selected the predictors DLelev, TFSth, and IntFlanker.
source: Compatible with the dominance analysis presented above, the model selected by the Lasso method contained the predictors DLelev, TFSth, and IntFlanker (see Table 1), and the highest regression coefficients were estimated for DLelev and TFSth.
evidence: This is a result from the Lasso variable selection procedure shown in Table 1.

claim: The Lasso procedure selected the predictor SSPcorr (working memory span).
source: In addition, the Lasso procedure selected the predictor SSPcorr (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the Lasso variable selection procedure shown in Table 1.

claim: The predictors DLelev and TFSth showed a significantly negative partial correlation with the SRS, controlling for age.
source: The predictors DLelev and TFSth showed a significantly negative partial correlation with the SRS, compatible with the results from ordinary least-squares (OLS) regression and the Lasso.
evidence: This is a result from the partial correlation analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The partial correlation coefficient for SSPcorr (working memory span) was significant.
source: As for the Lasso, the partial correlation coefficient for SSPcorr was also significant.
evidence: This is a result from the partial correlation analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The model relating SSQ scores to speech recognition score explained only a small, non-significant portion of the variance, R² = 0.137, p=0.17, N = 47.
source: The model explained only a small, non-significant portion of the variance, R2 = 0.137, p=0.17, N = 47.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the regression analysis of SSQ scores.

claim: Only the regression coefficient for the 'Other qualities' scale was significant, showing a positive relation between this SSQ subscore and the SRS.
source: Only the regression coefficient for the 'Other qualities' scale was significant, showing a positive relation between this SSQ subscore and the SRS (see Table 3).
evidence: This is a result from the regression analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: Persons reporting better hearing abilities on the SSQ 'Other qualities' scale tended to perform better in the spatial listening task.
source: Thus, persons reporting better hearing abilities on the SSQ 'Other qualities' scale tended to perform better in the spatial listening task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression result from Table 3.

claim: There was a significant negative relation between the DL-elevation and SSQspeech, controlling for age.
source: As seen in Table 2, the partial correlations controlling for age indicated a significant negative relation between the DL-elevation and SSQspeech, and between the IPD threshold in the TFS-LF test and SSQspatial and SSQqualities.
evidence: This is a result from the partial correlation analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: There was a significant negative relation between the IPD threshold in the TFS-LF test and SSQspatial, controlling for age.
source: As seen in Table 2, the partial correlations controlling for age indicated a significant negative relation between the DL-elevation and SSQspeech, and between the IPD threshold in the TFS-LF test and SSQspatial and SSQqualities.
evidence: This is a result from the partial correlation analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: There was a significant negative relation between the IPD threshold in the TFS-LF test and SSQqualities, controlling for age.
source: As seen in Table 2, the partial correlations controlling for age indicated a significant negative relation between the DL-elevation and SSQspeech, and between the IPD threshold in the TFS-LF test and SSQspatial and SSQqualities.
evidence: This is a result from the partial correlation analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The individual ability to selectively attend to an auditory target stimulus in the presence of distractors as well as the ability to attend to a visual target stimulus explained a significant portion of the variance in sentence identification performance with two interfering talkers.
source: In our experiment, the individual ability to selectively attend to an auditory target stimulus in the presence of distractors (measured in an intensity discrimination task under backward masking; Oberfeld et al., 2014) as well as the ability to attend to a visual target stimulus (measured in a Flanker task; Kramer and Jacobson, 1991) explained a significant portion of the variance in sentence identification performance with two interfering talkers.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Together, the two measures of selective attention explained approximately the same proportion of variance as the binaural TFS sensitivity.
source: Together, the two measures of selective attention explained approximately the same proportion of variance as the binaural TFS sensitivity, which was the predictor with the highest relative importance (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of variance explained by different predictors based on Table 1.

claim: Not only rather basic auditory factors like spatial hearing abilities contribute to individual differences in cocktail-party listening, but a general ability of focusing attention on a relevant target stimulus represents an additional important predictor.
source: These results are compatible with our hypothesis that not only rather basic auditory factors like spatial hearing abilities contribute to individual differences in cocktail-party listening, but that in the cognitive domain a general ability of focusing attention on a relevant target stimulus represents an additional important predictor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in relation to the hypothesis.

claim: In unaided hearing-impaired listeners (mean age about 66 years), word recognition performance in static background noise was positively related to performance in the 'Elevator counting with distraction' subtest of the Tests of Everyday Attention.
source: One of the few previous studies that measured selective attention in the presence of distractors (Gatehouse and Akeroyd, 2008) found that in unaided hearing-impaired listeners (mean age about 66 years) the word recognition performance in static background noise was positively related to performance in the 'Elevator counting with distraction' subtest of the Tests of Everyday Attention.
evidence: This is data from a cited study by Gatehouse and Akeroyd, 2008.

claim: In a study of subjects aged 55-84 years, a composite score for 'inhibition' that included the error rate in an incongruent condition of the Stroop color-word test was negatively correlated with sentence-final word recognition (controlling for age).
source: In a recent study (Cahana-Amitay et al., 2016), a composite score for 'inhibition' that included the error rate in an incongruent condition of the Stroop color-word test (Stroop, 1935) was negatively correlated with sentence-final word recognition (controlling for age) in a group of subjects ranging in age between 55 and 84 years.
evidence: This is data from a cited study by Cahana-Amitay et al., 2016.

claim: The working memory span did not show a strong relation to cocktail-party listening.
source: The working memory span did not show a strong relation to cocktail-party listening.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding working memory.

claim: Although the sentence identification task requires working memory for storing the sequence of five words, the performance on this task appeared to be more strongly limited by failures of selective attention than by memory aspects.
source: Thus, although the sentence identification task we presented requires working memory for storing the sequence of five words, the performance on this task appeared to be more strongly limited by failures of selective attention than by memory aspects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relative importance of different predictors.

claim: In older, hearing-impaired participants, working memory capacity and speech identification in noise are associated.
source: This result is compatible with previous data indicating that working memory capacity and speech identification in noise are associated in older, hearing-impaired participants (see Akeroyd, 2008), while in normal hearing subjects this correlation is weaker or even absent (Füllgrabe and Rosen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akeroyd, 2008 and Füllgrabe and Rosen, 2016.

claim: In normal hearing subjects, the correlation between working memory capacity and speech identification in noise is weaker or even absent.
source: This result is compatible with previous data indicating that working memory capacity and speech identification in noise are associated in older, hearing-impaired participants (see Akeroyd, 2008), while in normal hearing subjects this correlation is weaker or even absent (Füllgrabe and Rosen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Füllgrabe and Rosen, 2016.

claim: Working memory and attention are not independent.
source: In general, working memory and attention are not independent (Cowan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cowan et al., 2005.

claim: In a dichotic listening task, the probability of recognizing one's own name on the ignored channel was higher in participants with a low working memory span.
source: For instance, Conway et al. (2001) studied the probability that in a dichotic listening task participants recognize their own name on the ignored channel (Moray, 1959), and found that this probability was higher in participants with a low WM span.
evidence: This is data from a cited study by Conway et al., 2001.

claim: The working memory load affects speech understanding in a cocktail-party setting.
source: Also, the working memory load affects speech understanding in a cocktail-party setting (Francis, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Francis, 2010.

claim: The working memory span showed a marginally significant negative correlation (controlling for age) with the DL-elevation (auditory selective attention).
source: In line with these results, in our data the working memory span showed a marginally significant negative correlation (controlling for age) with the DL-elevation (auditory selective attention), see Table 2.
evidence: This is a result from the partial correlation analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The results confirm the association between binaural TFS sensitivity and speech identification in a spatial listening task.
source: Our results confirm the association between binaural TFS sensitivity for speech identification in a spatial listening task, compatible with earlier studies (Füllgrabe et al., 2014; Neher et al., 2011; Neher et al., 2012; Ruggles et al., 2011; Schoof and Rosen, 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of findings with reference to previous studies.

claim: The significant negative association between the IPD threshold and the SRS could be attributed to a reduced benefit from ITD cues in listeners with impaired binaural TFS sensitivity.
source: The significant negative association between the IPD threshold and the SRS could be attributed to a reduced benefit from ITD cues in listeners with impaired binaural TFS sensitivity, although a reduction in TFS sensitivity could be also associated with other perceptual impairments beyond sound source localization (Moore, 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the association with reference to a citation.

claim: A reduction in TFS sensitivity could be associated with other perceptual impairments beyond sound source localization.
source: The significant negative association between the IPD threshold and the SRS could be attributed to a reduced benefit from ITD cues in listeners with impaired binaural TFS sensitivity, although a reduction in TFS sensitivity could be also associated with other perceptual impairments beyond sound source localization (Moore, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moore, 2008.

claim: Spatial cues facilitate auditory streaming/grouping.
source: Spatial cues facilitate auditory streaming/grouping (e.g., Darwin and Hukin, 1999; David et al., 2015), selective attention (e.g., Ihlefeld and Shinn-Cunningham, 2008), and speech recognition (e.g., Culling et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spatial cues facilitate selective attention.
source: Spatial cues facilitate auditory streaming/grouping (e.g., Darwin and Hukin, 1999; David et al., 2015), selective attention (e.g., Ihlefeld and Shinn-Cunningham, 2008), and speech recognition (e.g., Culling et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ihlefeld and Shinn-Cunningham, 2008.

claim: Spatial cues facilitate speech recognition.
source: Spatial cues facilitate auditory streaming/grouping (e.g., Darwin and Hukin, 1999; David et al., 2015), selective attention (e.g., Ihlefeld and Shinn-Cunningham, 2008), and speech recognition (e.g., Culling et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Culling et al., 2004.

claim: The importance of spatial cues was reported to increase with the number of interfering sound sources.
source: The importance of spatial cues was reported to increase with the number of interfering sound sources (Yost et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yost et al., 1996.

claim: One should expect a smaller influence of TFS sensitivity in situations with only one interfering speaker compared to two.
source: Thus, one should expect a smaller influence of TFS sensitivity in situations with only one interfering speaker (compared to two as in the present study).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the relationship between number of interferers and importance of spatial cues.

claim: The simulated anechoic environment might have caused an overestimation of the importance of ITD cues.
source: Also, the simulated anechoic environment might have caused an overestimation of the importance of ITD cues.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential limitation of the study design.

claim: In a typical reverberant environment, spatial cues to sound source segregation are reduced.
source: In a typical reverberant environment, spatial cues to sound source segregation are reduced (e.g., Lavandier and Culling, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lavandier and Culling, 2010.

claim: The spatial separation of 25° between target and distractor speakers was larger than in some previous studies that used a separation of only 15°.
source: On the other hand, the spatial separation of 25° between target and distractor speakers was larger than in some previous studies that used a separation of only 15° (Ruggles et al., 2011, 2012, Ruggles and Shinn-Cunningham, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies with citations.

claim: The stronger ITD cues in the study might have reduced the importance of the sensory representation of the acoustic stimulus for task performance, which would emphasize the relative importance of central factors.
source: The corresponding stronger ITD cues in our study might have reduced the importance of the sensory representation of the acoustic stimulus for task performance, which would emphasize the relative importance of central factors.
evidence: This is speculation about how the study design might have affected the results.

claim: In cocktail-party situations in daily life, the spatial separation between the target speakers and competing speakers will often be even larger than 25°.
source: Note that in cocktail-party situations in daily life, the spatial separation between the target speakers and competing speakers will often be even larger than 25°.
evidence: This is a statement about typical real-world conditions.

claim: The self-report measures of hearing abilities (SSQ scores) showed only weak associations with performance in the cocktail-party listening task (controlling for age).
source: The self-report measures of hearing abilities (SSQ scores) showed only weak associations with performance in the cocktail-party listening task (controlling for age).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding SSQ scores.

claim: In hearing-impaired listeners, some earlier studies reported rather small correlations between SSQ scores and speech identification in static or amplitude-modulated background noise, even without controlling for age.
source: In hearing-impaired listeners, some earlier studies (Gatehouse and Akeroyd, 2008; Heinrich et al., 2015) also reported rather small correlations between SSQ scores and speech identification in static or amplitude-modulated background noise, even without controlling for age.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gatehouse and Akeroyd, 2008 and Heinrich et al., 2015.

claim: Füllgrabe et al. (2014) found no correlation between SSQ scores and speech-in-noise perception in audiometrically normal-hearing listeners.
source: Füllgrabe et al. (2014) found no correlation between SSQ scores and speech-in-noise perception in audiometrically normal-hearing listeners.
evidence: This is data from a cited study by Füllgrabe et al., 2014.

claim: The sample size in the study was larger than in some previous experiments.
source: Compared to previous studies on predictors of cocktail-party listening, our experiments introduced several methodological improvements. The sample size in our study was larger than in some previous experiments, so that it was possible to measure the influence of several variables on sentence identification in noise, without first combining predictors into a small number of factors.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous research.

claim: Multiple linear regression accounts for correlations among the predictors.
source: Multiple linear regression accounts for correlations among the predictors (Gauss, 1821), while interpreting pairwise correlations is extremely difficult for a large set of intercorrelated predictors.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical methodology with a citation to Gauss, 1821.

claim: The reliability of the measured variables was acceptable to high in most cases.
source: Unlike most previous studies, we also report the reliability of the measured variables, which in most cases was acceptable to high.
evidence: This is a summary of the reliability analyses reported in the study.

claim: The Lasso method was proposed to avoid some of the problems of forward or backward selection in stepwise regression.
